1:2.t: The Amalekite's story differs from 1 Samuel 31:3-6, where Saul falls on his own sword. He probably lied, hoping for a reward (see 4:10).

1:10.t: "Band": the KJV's "bracelet", an armband worn as a sign of royalty.

1:18.t: "The use of the bow": the KJV adds "the use of" in italics; the Hebrew reads only "the Bow", which may be the name of the lament that follows. The Book of Jashar ("the upright") was an early collection of poems, also quoted at Joshua 10:13.

1:21.t: "Fields that yield offerings": the KJV's "fields of offerings". "Defiled": the KJV's "vilely cast away". Shields were rubbed with oil before battle, so Saul's shield lies unoiled, like the king who is no longer anointed.

2:8.t: Ish-bosheth means "man of shame". His name is given as Eshbaal ("man of Baal") at 1 Chronicles 8:33; later scribes seem to have replaced "Baal" with "bosheth", shame. The same is true of Mephibosheth (4:4; Merib-baal in 1 Chronicles 8:34) and Jerubbesheth (11:21; Jerubbaal, that is, Gideon, Judges 6:32).
Mahanaim: a town east of the Jordan, out of reach of the Philistines.

2:12.t: Mahanaim: a town east of the Jordan, out of reach of the Philistines.

2:29.t: Mahanaim: a town east of the Jordan, out of reach of the Philistines.
"The Arabah": the KJV's "the plain", the dry lowland of the Jordan valley and the Dead Sea (see 1 Samuel 23:24). "The whole Bithron": the Hebrew may mean a ravine or "the whole morning".

2:16.t: Helkath-hazzurim means "field of flints" or "field of sword edges".

3:7.t: Taking a former king's concubine was a claim to his throne (compare 16:21-22 and 1 Kings 2:22), which is why Ish-bosheth is alarmed.

3:8.t: "Dog's head": a term of contempt, meaning a worthless or traitorous person.

"Kindness", "loyalty", "steadfast love" (Hebrew hesed): loyal, committed love that keeps its promises, especially within a covenant; no single English word covers it (see Genesis 24:27). When people show hesed to one another we write "kindness" or "loyalty" (2:5, 3:8, 9:1, 10:2, 16:17); when it is God's we write "steadfast love" (2:6). David asks to show "the steadfast love of God" (9:3) to Saul's house, the faithful love God shows, keeping his oath to Jonathan (1 Samuel 20:14-15). At 15:20 David's blessing on Ittai, "May steadfast love and faithfulness be with you", is a prayer that God's hesed and emet (firmness, reliability) will go with him; the Greek adds "may the LORD show you".

3:29.t: "A discharge or a skin disease": the KJV's "an issue, or that is a leper". Both conditions made a person ritually unclean, and the Hebrew for "leper" covers a range of skin diseases, not modern leprosy (see Leviticus 13 and 15). "Leans on a crutch": the KJV's "leaneth on a staff"; the Hebrew may also mean "holds a spindle", that is, does women's work.

3:31.t: "Bier": the stretcher on which a body was carried to burial.

4:6.t: "As though they were getting wheat": the Greek reads differently: the woman at the door was cleaning wheat and fell asleep, so they slipped in.

5:6.t: "The blind and the lame": the Jebusites boasted that even the blind and lame could hold off David. The saying in verse 8 may come from this taunt.

5:8.t: "Water shaft": the KJV's "gutter". The Hebrew tsinnor probably means a water tunnel into the city, though it may mean a grappling hook.

5:9.t: "The Millo": the KJV keeps the Hebrew word, which means "filling", probably a terraced earthwork on the slope of the city.

5:21.t: "Burned them": the KJV's "burned them"; the Hebrew reads "carried them off", and 1 Chronicles 14:12 says they were burned.

5:23.t: "Mulberry trees": as in the KJV. The Hebrew word may mean balsam or poplar trees.

6:3.t: "At Gibeah": the KJV's "in Gibeah"; the Hebrew can mean "on the hill".

6:5.t: "Cypress wood": the KJV's "fir wood". 1 Chronicles 13:8 reads "with all their might and with songs". "Lyres, harps, tambourines, rattles and cymbals": the KJV's "harps, psalteries, timbrels, cornets and cymbals".

6:6.t: Nacon: the KJV's "Nachon". It is called Chidon at 1 Chronicles 13:9.

6:7.t: "Irreverence": the KJV's "error". The law allowed only the Levites to carry the ark, on poles, and forbade anyone to touch it (Numbers 4:15).

6:14.t: "Linen ephod": a simple priestly garment, probably a kind of apron or vest (see 1 Samuel 2:18).

6:19.t: "Cake of raisins": the KJV's "flagon of wine"; the Hebrew word means a pressed cake of raisins or dates.

6:20.t: "Uncovering himself": David's dancing in a short linen ephod exposed him in Michal's eyes.

7:2.t: "House of cedar": a fine palace, paneled with cedar (5:11).

7:14.t: "The rod of men, with blows inflicted by human beings": the KJV's "with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the children of men", meaning God will discipline him through human agents.

"I will be his Father, and he will be My son": in the ancient Near East a great king called a loyal vassal his son. God takes the king of David's line into this close relationship, with both care and discipline. Hebrews 1:5 applies the verse to Christ. "Father" is capitalized because God is speaking of Himself.

7:18.t: "Sat before the LORD": in the tent where the ark was kept (6:17).

7:19.t: "Is this the way You deal with mankind?": the KJV's "is this the manner of man?" The Hebrew is hard; it may also mean "this is instruction for mankind".

7:23.t: "Before Your people ... from the nations and their gods": the KJV wording is kept; the Hebrew is compressed, and 1 Chronicles 17:21 reads "by driving out nations before Your people".

8:1.t: Metheg-ammah means "the bridle of the mother city", perhaps the control of Gath (1 Chronicles 18:1 reads "Gath and its towns").

8:3.t: Hadadezer: the KJV spells it Hadadezer here and Hadarezer at 10:16. "Restore his control": the KJV's "recover his border".

8:4.t: "700 horsemen": as in the Hebrew and the KJV. 1 Chronicles 18:4 reads 7,000.

10:6.t: "Become a stench": the KJV's "stank before David" (compare 1 Samuel 13:4). Beth-rehob, Zobah, Maacah and Tob were Aramean kingdoms north and east of Israel. Tob: the KJV's "Ishtob", read as "men of Tob".

8:13.t: "Arameans": as in the KJV. Some Hebrew manuscripts and the Greek read "Edomites", which fits the Valley of Salt and 1 Chronicles 18:12.

8:17.t: "Ahimelech the son of Abiathar": as in the Hebrew and the KJV; elsewhere Abiathar is the son of Ahimelech (1 Samuel 22:20). "Secretary": the KJV's "scribe".

8:18.t: Cherethites and Pelethites: foreign soldiers in David's guard, probably from Crete and Philistia; the Cherethites were a people living near the Philistines (see 1 Samuel 30:14). "Chief officials": the KJV's "chief rulers"; the Hebrew word usually means priests.

9:4.t: Lo-debar: a town east of the Jordan; the name sounds like "no pasture" or "nothing".

9:8.t: "Dead dog": a phrase of deep self-humbling (compare 1 Samuel 24:14).

10:4.t: "At their buttocks": the KJV's "even to their buttocks". Shaving half the beard and exposing them was a deep insult to the envoys and to David.

10:18.t: "700 chariots": as in the Hebrew and the KJV; 1 Chronicles 19:18 reads 7,000. "40,000 horsemen": 1 Chronicles 19:18 reads "foot soldiers".

11:1.t: "In the spring": the KJV's "after the year was expired", that is, at the turn of the year, when the rains ended and armies could march.

11:4.t: "She had just purified herself from her uncleanness": the ritual washing seven days after her monthly period (Leviticus 15:19-28). It shows that she was not already pregnant and that the child was David's.

"Took her" (Hebrew laqach): the verb is the ordinary word for take, fetch or marry, and it is used of a king's power in Samuel's warning (1 Samuel 8:11-16, "he will take"). The text says David "sent messengers and took her", and Nathan's parable (12:4) and judgment (12:9) lay the guilt on David alone. The verse does not say what Bathsheba felt; interpreters differ on how far she could have refused a king, but the narrator's blame falls on David.

11:8.t: "Wash your feet": go home and rest; it may also hint at sleeping with his wife.

11:11.t: "As surely as your soul lives": the KJV's "as thy soul liveth", a solemn oath meaning "as surely as you live". The Hebrew nephesh means the living self, the whole person (see Genesis 2:7).

11:21.t: Jerubbesheth is Gideon, also called Jerubbaal (Judges 6:32, 9:50-54). Later scribes seem to have replaced "Baal" in names with "bosheth", shame (see 2:8).

12:6.t: "Four times": the law for a stolen sheep (Exodus 22:1). The Greek reads "sevenfold".

12:8.t: "Your master's wives": the harem of a king passed to the one who took his throne; taking a former king's concubine was a claim to his throne (see 3:7).

12:11.t: "In broad daylight": the KJV's "in the sight of this sun". This is fulfilled at 16:21-22.

12:14.t: "Given the enemies of the LORD great cause to show contempt": as in the KJV. Some Hebrew scholars think "the enemies of" was added by scribes to avoid writing "you have despised the LORD".

12:24.t: Solomon sounds like shalom, "peace". Jedidiah means "loved by the LORD".

12:27.t: "The city's water supply": the KJV's "the city of waters", probably the lower part of Rabbah that held its water source.

12:30.t: "Their king's crown": the Hebrew malkam can also be read Milcom, the god of the Ammonites, so some modern Bibles read "the crown of Milcom", taken from the idol. KJV: "a talent of gold".

12:31.t: "Put them to the saws, the iron picks and the iron axes, and made them pass through the brick kiln": the KJV's "put them under saws, and under harrows of iron ... and made them pass through the brickkiln". This can mean that the captives were tortured, or, as most modern scholars read it, that they were set to forced labor with these tools and at the brick kilns.

13:3.t: Shimeah is called Shammah at 1 Samuel 16:9. "Shrewd": the KJV's "subtil", crafty.

13:6.t: "Cakes": the Hebrew word sounds like "heart", perhaps heart-shaped cakes.

13:8.t: "Cakes": the Hebrew word sounds like "heart", perhaps heart-shaped cakes.

13:10.t: "Cakes": the Hebrew word sounds like "heart", perhaps heart-shaped cakes.

13:16.t: "Sending me away is a greater wrong": under the law a man who violated a virgin was required to marry her and could never divorce her (Deuteronomy 22:28-29).

13:18.t: "Long robe with sleeves": the KJV's "garment of divers colours", the same phrase as Joseph's robe (Genesis 37:3). The Hebrew probably means a long robe reaching to the wrists and ankles.

13:21.t: The Greek and the Dead Sea Scrolls add: "but he did not punish his son Amnon, because he loved him, for he was his firstborn." The KJV does not include it.

13:23.t: Baal-hazor: a hill north of Jerusalem. Sheep-shearing was a time of feasting (1 Samuel 25:8).

13:39.t: "King David's spirit longed": the KJV's "the soul of king David longed". The Hebrew is unclear; some read "the king's anger against Absalom faded".

14:2.t: Tekoa: the KJV spells it Tekoah. It was Amos's town (Amos 1:1).

14:7.t: "The last coal": a picture of the last surviving son, the one ember left to keep the family's fire alive.

14:11.t: "Avenger of blood": the KJV's "revengers of blood", the relative whose duty was to avenge a killing (Numbers 35:19).

14:14.t: "God does not show favoritism": the KJV's "neither doth God respect any person". The Hebrew reads "God does not take away life", which many modern Bibles follow.

14:17.t: "Give me rest": the KJV's "be comfortable", that is, bring comfort and settle the matter.

14:26.t: KJV: "two hundred shekels after the king's weight". The royal weight may have differed from the common shekel.

15:1.t: "Fifty men to run ahead of him": a royal escort, as Samuel had warned (1 Samuel 8:11).

15:7.t: "At the end of forty years": as in the Hebrew and the KJV. The Greek and Syriac read "four years", which most modern Bibles follow.

15:8.t: "Aram": the KJV's "Syria"; Geshur was a small Aramean kingdom.

15:12.t: Giloh was a town in the hill country of Judah. Ahithophel was probably Bathsheba's grandfather (11:3, 23:34).

15:17.t: "At a place some distance away": the KJV's "in a place that was far off". The Hebrew reads "at the far house", perhaps the last house at the edge of the city.

15:18.t: Gittites: men from Gath, the Philistine city, who had followed David since his years there.

15:23.t: "The Kidron Valley": the KJV's "the brook Kidron", the valley east of Jerusalem between the city and the Mount of Olives.

15:24.t: "Abiathar went up": as in the KJV. The Hebrew can also mean "offered sacrifices".

15:28.t: "Plains of the wilderness": as in the KJV. The Hebrew can also be read "fords of the wilderness", the crossings of the Jordan.

15:30.t: Covering the head and walking barefoot were signs of mourning. "Mount of Olives": the KJV's "mount Olivet".

15:32.t: "Hushai the Archite": of the Archites, a clan living near Bethel (Joshua 16:2).

15:37.t: "David's friend": a title for a close royal adviser.

16:16.t: "David's friend": a title for a close royal adviser.
"Long live the king": the KJV's "God save the king"; the Hebrew is "may the king live" (see 1 Samuel 10:24).

16:3.t: "Your master's grandson": the KJV's "thy master's son"; Mephibosheth was Saul's grandson. Compare 19:24-30, where Mephibosheth gives a different account.

16:7.t: "Man of blood": the KJV's "bloody man", meaning a murderer. "Worthless man": the KJV's "man of Belial". The Hebrew beliyaal is not a name here; the word probably means "without worth" or "good for nothing", and describes scoundrels and troublemakers (see 1 Samuel 1:16).

16:10.t: "What do I have to do with you?": an expression meaning "this is not your concern" or "we do not see this the same way".

19:22.t: "What do I have to do with you?": an expression meaning "this is not your concern" or "we do not see this the same way".

16:12.t: "My misery": the KJV's "mine affliction". The Hebrew text reads "my guilt"; the Hebrew margin and ancient versions read "my eye", meaning my tears.

16:21.t: Sleeping with the king's concubines in public was a claim to the throne and a final break with David (see 3:7), fulfilling 12:11.

17:3.t: "The return of everyone depends on the man you are seeking": the KJV's "the man whom thou seekest is as if all returned". The Hebrew is unclear.

17:13.t: "Valley": the KJV's "river"; the Hebrew word means a ravine or stream bed.

17:17.t: En-rogel: a spring just south of Jerusalem. "Servant girl": the KJV's "wench", which in 1611 simply meant a girl or young woman.

17:19.t: "Grain": the KJV's "ground corn", meaning crushed grain spread out to dry.

17:20.t: "Stream": the KJV's "brook of water". The Hebrew word is rare.

17:25.t: Amasa was David's nephew, the son of his sister Abigail. "Ithra the Israelite": 1 Chronicles 2:17 reads "Jether the Ishmaelite". Nahash here is not the Ammonite king.

17:28.t: "Roasted grain": the KJV's "parched corn" (corn means grain). "Roasted seeds": the KJV's "parched pulse", the seeds of peas or beans.

18:3.t: "Worth 10,000 of us": the KJV's "worth ten thousand of us". Some Hebrew manuscripts read "but there are 10,000 like us".

18:8.t: "The forest devoured more people": the rough, wooded ground with its ravines and thickets killed more than the fighting did.

18:11.t: KJV: "ten shekels of silver". "Belt": the KJV's "girdle"; a soldier's belt was a mark of honor.

18:12.t: KJV: "a thousand shekels of silver". "For my sake, protect": the KJV's "Beware that none touch"; the Hebrew reads "watch, whoever you are, over the young man".

18:14.t: "Spears": the KJV's "darts"; the Hebrew means staffs or sticks, perhaps sharpened.

18:18.t: "Absalom's Monument": the KJV's "Absalom's place"; the Hebrew word means a hand, here a marker or memorial (see 1 Samuel 15:12). Absalom says he has no son, though 14:27 names three; they may have died young.

18:21.t: Cushi: the KJV treats the word as a name. The Hebrew means "the Cushite", a man from Cush, south of Egypt.

18:22.t: "You will get no reward for the news": the KJV's "seeing that thou hast no tidings ready". The Hebrew means that this news will bring no reward.

18:23.t: "The way of the plain": the Jordan valley, a longer but easier route.

18:33.t: This is 19:1 in Hebrew Bibles, and the verse numbers of chapter 19 run one higher in Hebrew.

19:11.t: "What all Israel is saying has reached the king at his palace": the KJV wording is kept. The Greek places this clause at the end of verse 10.

19:13.t: Amasa had commanded Absalom's army (17:25); David's offer is meant to win over Judah.

19:18.t: "A ferry boat went across": as in the KJV. The Hebrew may mean "they crossed the ford".

19:20.t: "House of Joseph": the northern tribes, of which Ephraim and Manasseh, the sons of Joseph, were the chief.

19:24.t: "Grandson": the KJV's "son"; Mephibosheth was Saul's grandson. "Mustache": the KJV's "beard", the hair of the upper lip. Neglecting these was a sign of mourning.

19:35.t: "What is good and what is not": the KJV's "good and evil", meaning pleasant and unpleasant.

19:43.t: "Ten shares": the ten northern tribes. "Spoke even more harshly": the KJV's "were fiercer". This quarrel leads to Sheba's revolt in chapter 20.

20:1.t: "Worthless man": the KJV's "man of Belial". The Hebrew beliyaal is not a name here; the word probably means "without worth" or "good for nothing", and describes scoundrels and troublemakers (see 1 Samuel 1:16). "Every man to his tents": go home; the same cry is raised at the split of the kingdom (1 Kings 12:16).

20:8.t: "Joab was wearing his military tunic": the KJV's "Joab's garment that he had put on was girded unto him". The sword fell out, perhaps on purpose, so that Joab could pick it up without alarming Amasa.

20:10.t: "In the stomach": the KJV's "in the fifth rib" (see 2:23, 3:27).

20:14.t: "All the Berites": as in the KJV. The Hebrew is uncertain; the Greek reads "all the Bichrites", Sheba's own clan.

20:15.t: Beth-maacah: the KJV spells it Beth-maachah. "Stood against the outer wall": the KJV's "it stood in the trench", the defensive rampart around the wall.

20:18.t: "Be sure to ask for advice at Abel": Abel was known for its wise counsel.

20:19.t: "A mother in Israel": a leading town, with smaller towns around it as its daughters.

20:24.t: "Forced labor": the KJV's "the tribute"; the Hebrew means labor gangs.

20:26.t: "Chief official": the KJV's "chief ruler"; the Hebrew word usually means priest (see 8:18).

21:1.t: "Sought the face of the LORD": the KJV's "enquired of the LORD". Saul's attack on the Gibeonites broke the oath of Joshua 9:15-20 and is not recorded elsewhere.

21:6.t: "Hang": the Hebrew may mean impale or expose the bodies.

21:9.t: "Hang": the Hebrew may mean impale or expose the bodies.

21:8.t: "Michal": as in most Hebrew manuscripts and the KJV. Merab, not Michal, married Adriel (1 Samuel 18:19), and a few Hebrew and Greek manuscripts read Merab, which most modern Bibles follow. The KJV's "brought up for" tries to reconcile the two; the Hebrew reads "bore to".

21:10.t: "Until the rain fell": from the barley harvest in April until the autumn rains, a vigil of perhaps six months.

21:14.t: Zela: the KJV spells it Zelah. "God answered their prayers for the land": the KJV's "God was intreated for the land" (also 24:25).

21:16.t: "The giant": the Hebrew is rapha, perhaps the ancestor of the Rephaim, a race of very tall people (Deuteronomy 2:11). KJV: "three hundred shekels of brass".

21:18.t: "The giant": the Hebrew is rapha, perhaps the ancestor of the Rephaim, a race of very tall people (Deuteronomy 2:11). KJV: "three hundred shekels of brass".
Sibbecai: the KJV spells it Sibbechai.

21:20.t: "The giant": the Hebrew is rapha, perhaps the ancestor of the Rephaim, a race of very tall people (Deuteronomy 2:11). KJV: "three hundred shekels of brass".

21:22.t: "The giant": the Hebrew is rapha, perhaps the ancestor of the Rephaim, a race of very tall people (Deuteronomy 2:11). KJV: "three hundred shekels of brass".

21:17.t: "The lamp of Israel": the king as the light and hope of the nation.

21:19.t: "The brother of Goliath": the KJV adds "the brother of" in italics, from 1 Chronicles 20:5, which names him Lahmi. The Hebrew here reads "killed Goliath the Gittite". Jaare-oregim may be a copying error; "oregim" means "weavers" and appears later in the verse.

21:21.t: Shimeah: the KJV spells it Shimea here; he is the brother of David named at 13:3 and 1 Samuel 16:9 (Shammah).

22:1.t: This song appears again, with small differences, as Psalm 18.

22:3.t: "The strength of my salvation": the KJV's "the horn of my salvation", a picture of strength and honor taken from a strong animal's horns (see 1 Samuel 2:1).

22:5.t: "Wicked men": the KJV's "ungodly men"; the Hebrew is beliyaal, which probably means "without worth" or "good for nothing" (see 1 Samuel 1:16), here perhaps "destruction".

22:6.t: "The grave": the KJV's "hell"; the Hebrew is Sheol, the place of the dead, pictured as deep under the earth (see Genesis 37:35). "Confronted": the KJV's "prevented", meaning came before me (also 22:19).

22:27.t: "Shrewd": the KJV's "unsavoury"; the Hebrew means God outwits the crooked.

22:30.t: "Charge against a troop": the KJV's "run through a troop".

22:35.t: "Bronze": the KJV's "steel"; the Hebrew means bronze.

22:36.t: "Gentleness": the KJV's word. The Hebrew may mean "Your answering" or "Your help".

22:41.t: "Made my enemies turn their backs to me": the KJV's "given me the necks of mine enemies", a picture of enemies in flight.

23:1.t: "Sweet psalmist of Israel": the KJV's words are kept. The Hebrew can also mean "the favorite of the songs of Israel" or "the delight of Israel's strong One".

23:5.t: "Though my house is not so with God": as in the KJV. Many modern Bibles read the line as a question: "Is not my house like this with God?"

"Forever" (Hebrew olam): olam means a long, unseen span of time, far into the future or the past, and it often means truly forever, especially of God. It can also mean "for the lifetime of" or "for all generations" (Exodus 21:6). The promise to David is the basis of the later hope of a Messiah from his line (Psalm 89:3-4, Isaiah 9:7, Luke 1:32-33). We translate "forever", as the KJV does.

"Everlasting covenant" (Hebrew berit olam): olam means a long, unseen span of time, often truly forever (see 7:13 and 1 Samuel 18:3). David calls God's promise of chapter 7, that his house and kingdom would stand forever, a covenant, though the word is not used there. It stands beside the covenants with Noah (Genesis 9:16) and Abraham (Genesis 17:7).

23:6.t: "Worthless men": the KJV's "sons of Belial". The Hebrew beliyaal is not a name here; the word probably means "without worth" or "good for nothing", and describes scoundrels and troublemakers (see 1 Samuel 1:16).

23:8.t: "The Tahchemonite who sat in the seat of honor ... Adino the Eznite": as in the KJV. The Hebrew reads "Josheb-basshebeth a Tahchemonite", and 1 Chronicles 11:11 names him Jashobeam. "800": 1 Chronicles 11:11 reads 300.

23:9.t: Dodo: the KJV's spelling, also read Dodai.

23:13.t: "Thirty chiefs": David's elite band of warriors, listed in 23:24-39.

23:16.t: "Poured it out to the LORD": as a drink offering. David would not drink what had cost his men their lives to bring.

23:18.t: "Three": as in most Hebrew manuscripts and the KJV. Two Hebrew manuscripts and the Syriac read "thirty", which many modern Bibles follow.

23:20.t: "Lionlike warriors": the KJV's "lionlike men". The Hebrew word ariel is uncertain; it may be a name or mean great champions.

23:21.t: "An impressive man": the KJV's "a goodly man". 1 Chronicles 11:23 gives his height as about 2.3 meters (five cubits).

23:27.t: Anathothite: the KJV spells it Anethothite.

23:34.t: Maacathite: the KJV spells it Maachathite. Eliam may be Bathsheba's father (11:3).

23:39.t: "Thirty-seven in all": the thirty, with the three and other leaders, counted together.

24:1.t: "He stirred up David": 1 Chronicles 21:1 says Satan stirred him up. The two accounts together show that God allowed Satan to test David as a judgment on Israel. "Count": the KJV's "number". A census was a military muster, and counting the army as his own strength showed David's pride.

24:5.t: "South of the town": the KJV's "on the right side of the city"; facing east, the right hand is the south. "Valley of Gad": the KJV's "the river of Gad".

24:6.t: Tahtim-hodshi and Dan-jaan are uncertain place names. Sidon: the KJV spells it Zidon.

24:7.t: "Negev": the KJV's "south", the dry southern region of Judah (see 1 Samuel 27:10).

24:9.t: "800,000 ... 500,000": 1 Chronicles 21:5 gives 1,100,000 and 470,000; the two lists may have counted differently.

24:10.t: "David's conscience troubled him": the KJV's "David's heart smote him" (see 1 Samuel 24:5).

24:13.t: "Seven years": as in the Hebrew and the KJV. The Greek and 1 Chronicles 21:12 read three years, which matches the three months and three days.

24:16.t: Araunah is called Ornan at 1 Chronicles 21:15. His threshing floor became the site of Solomon's temple (2 Chronicles 3:1).

"Relented" (Hebrew nacham): the KJV's "repented him of the evil". Nacham means to be sorry, grieved or moved to change course, not an admission of a mistake (see Genesis 6:6 and 1 Samuel 15:11). God was moved to stop the disaster; "evil" here means harm, not wrongdoing.

24:22.t: "Threshing sledges": heavy wooden boards studded with stones, dragged over grain.

24:23.t: "Like a king": as in the KJV. The Hebrew reads "Araunah the king", which can mean "O king", as many modern Bibles read.

24:24.t: KJV: "fifty shekels of silver". 1 Chronicles 21:25 gives 600 shekels of gold, perhaps for the whole site and not only the threshing floor and oxen.

1:19.t: David's lament (Hebrew qinah, a funeral song): the poem uses the rhythm of a dirge, with a long line followed by a shorter, falling one. "How the mighty have fallen!" (eik naphelu gibborim) opens, centers and closes it (1:19, 1:25, 1:27). "Your glory" (1:19, the KJV's "the beauty of Israel") translates tsevi, which also means gazelle, so the line may picture Saul and Jonathan as Israel's graceful gazelle lying dead on the heights. We keep "glory" with the KJV's sense and note the other.

1:26.t: "Your love for me" (Hebrew ahavah): ahav covers love of every kind, between family members, friends, spouses, and between God and His people (see Genesis 22:2 and 1 Samuel 18:1). Here it is the love of a sworn friend and covenant partner, which David says surpassed even the devotion of women. The word does not in itself imply anything sexual; it is the same word used of Jonathan's loyal love at 1 Samuel 18:1-3. Readers who see more in it rely on modern assumptions the text does not support.

2:5.t: "Kindness", "loyalty", "steadfast love" (Hebrew hesed): loyal, committed love that keeps its promises, especially within a covenant; no single English word covers it (see Genesis 24:27). When people show hesed to one another we write "kindness" or "loyalty" (2:5, 3:8, 9:1, 10:2, 16:17); when it is God's we write "steadfast love" (2:6). David asks to show "the steadfast love of God" (9:3) to Saul's house, the faithful love God shows, keeping his oath to Jonathan (1 Samuel 20:14-15). At 15:20 David's blessing on Ittai, "May steadfast love and faithfulness be with you", is a prayer that God's hesed and emet (firmness, reliability) will go with him; the Greek adds "may the LORD show you".

3:33.t: "As a fool dies" (Hebrew nabal, the name of the fool in 1 Samuel 25:25): the nabal is not slow-witted but morally senseless, a man who lives as if there were no God (Psalm 14:1). David's lament says Abner did not die as such a man deserves, in a fair judgment, but by treachery. The same root is used of Tamar's plea at 13:12-13.

7:5.t: "House" (Hebrew bayit): the chapter turns on the word's two meanings. David wants to build God a house, a temple (7:5); God answers that He will build David a house, a dynasty (7:11, 7:27). David's son will build the house for God's name (7:13), and David's house and kingdom will stand forever (7:16). We keep "house" throughout so the reader can see the wordplay.

"Forever" (Hebrew olam): olam means a long, unseen span of time, far into the future or the past, and it often means truly forever, especially of God. It can also mean "for the lifetime of" or "for all generations" (Exodus 21:6). The promise to David is the basis of the later hope of a Messiah from his line (Psalm 89:3-4, Isaiah 9:7, Luke 1:32-33). We translate "forever", as the KJV does.

"Steadfast love" (Hebrew hesed, God's loyal covenant love) "to His anointed" (Hebrew meshicho, the word that gives us Messiah; see 1 Samuel 2:10): the song ends with God's covenant love for David and his offspring forever, the promise of chapter 7.

7:15.t: "My steadfast love" (Hebrew hesed): loyal, committed love that keeps its promises, especially within a covenant (see Genesis 24:27). Here it is God's covenant faithfulness, which He promises never to take from David's son as He took it from Saul. This is God's hesed, so we write "steadfast love".

12:13.t: "The LORD has taken away your sin" (Hebrew he'evir, "caused to pass over", the KJV's "put away"): God removes the guilt so that David will not die as the law required for adultery and murder (Leviticus 20:10, 24:17). The consequences still follow (12:10-14). Psalm 51 is traditionally linked to this moment.

13:12.t: "Disgraceful thing", "disgraceful fools" (Hebrew nebalah, nabal): the nabal is not slow-witted but morally senseless, a man who lives as if there were no God (see 3:33). Nebalah is a serious, shameful crime against the community, used of rape at Genesis 34:7 and Judges 19:23. The KJV's "folly" and "fools" sound too light today.

22:26.t: "The loyal" (Hebrew hasid, one who shows hesed): we write "loyal" because it is a person's hesed; God answers loyalty with loyalty. The KJV's "merciful" is narrower than the Hebrew.
